article.articleHeadline: Lagos orders hygiene upgrade in hotels, clubs over Ebola alert
article.articleSummary: Lagos State Safety Commission orders hotels, nightclubs, event centres, lounges and other social venues to strengthen hygiene and safety due to Ebola alerts in Central and East Africa. No confirmed Ebola case in Lagos or Nigeria, but as a major international travel hub, proactive measures are mandated. Institutions must install hand hygiene stations at entry points and common areas, increase cleaning with hospital-grade disinfectants on high-touch surfaces, train staff to recognise illness, perform daily health checks, and enforce a strict stay-at-home policy for fever. A temporary on-site holding area for isolation pending medical evacuation must be designated; crowd management and adequate ventilation are required. Health hotlines provided; inspectors will monitor compliance. Outbreak context: Bundibugyo Ebola virus with 43 confirmed deaths (42 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 1 in Uganda) and 349 suspected deaths as of May 30; origin linked to fruit bats, with human infection via contact with infected wildlife secretions.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Extreme weather triggers a surge in illnesses; IDAI urges parents to be vigilant.
article.articleSummary: Jakarta, Indonesia — IDAI warns that climate change, heat, air pollution, floods, droughts, and shifting seasons are driving a surge in illnesses among children. Because their immune systems and organs are still developing, youngsters are particularly vulnerable to extreme weather. The report notes increases in respiratory infections and diarrhea with severe dehydration due to heat waves, as well as broader rises in infectious and non-infectious conditions. Warmer temperatures and irregular rainfall expand transmission of mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue fever and malaria. Heavy rainfall and floods raise leptospirosis risk, and sanitation disruption heightens skin diseases. Prolonged drought threatens child nutrition and growth. Parents should monitor air quality, ensure hydration and handwashing, maintain 3M Plus mosquito control at home, and keep up-to-date immunizations, including PCV and influenza where possible. Media briefing on 9 June 2026, Jakarta.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: An infectious-disease doctor explains how to protect yourself from hantavirus.
article.articleSummary: As of June 10, 2026, there is no broad, licensed universal vaccine for hantaviruses. Protection relies on good hygiene, rodent control, and disinfection of premises. Inactivated vaccines for specific hantavirus strains exist only in China and South Korea. Hantavirus infection occurs after contact with wild rodents from Muridae and Cricetidae families, with the virus shed in feces, urine, and saliva. A deadly outbreak linked to the MV Hondius—traveling from Argentina to Cabo Verde—killed three people. The vessel arrived at the Canary Islands on May 10, after which evacuated passengers were moved and the ship proceeded to Rotterdam. The report underscores non-pharmaceutical measures as the main defense pending broader vaccine coverage.

article.articleHeadline: 汛期谨防感染血吸虫病
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Take precautions to prevent schistosomiasis infection during the flood season.
article.articleSummary: As of June 10, 2026, Nanchang city, China, entering the flood season (April–October), faces rising risk of schistosomiasis infection during water activities. The Nanchang City Center for Disease Control and Prevention warns that cercariae from infected Oncomelania snails can penetrate unprotected skin within about 10 seconds. High-risk activities include water-related work, flood relief, and outdoor recreation; anglers should be cautious as touching fish, wading barefoot, washing hands, or gear wet with water may expose skin. Acute schistosomiasis typically presents in first-time infections with fever that rises in the afternoon, peaks in the evening, and sweats at night; hepatomegaly is common, with tender liver and possible splenomegaly in severe cases. Preventive measures: avoid water in snail-infested zones with warning signs; boil or disinfect drinking water; wear long boots, waterproof pants, and gloves; apply anti-cercariae cream before exposure. Public urged vigilance and timely treatment.

article.articleSummary: East Democratic Republic of Congo Ebola outbreak surpasses 550 confirmed cases and 101 deaths across Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu; overall case fatality 17.7%. Ituri remains the epicenter with about 500 cases (roughly 95% of total). The outbreak was declared May 15, marking the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC since 1976. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or treatment. Africa CDC reports pending Ebola tests reduced from over 1,100 to 116 by June 3, with 397 confirmed cases as samples were processed; Uganda reports 16 cases and 1 death. WHO and Africa CDC plan US$518 million over six months to bolster preparedness and response in Africa; the EU adds €5 million to support control efforts. On June 8, WHO warned of rapid spread, wider geographic reach, and cross-border transmission, with very high risk in DRC and high risk in Uganda and neighboring countries.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Nearly 600 Ebola cases recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
article.articleSummary: 598 confirmed Ebola virus disease cases, 115 deaths, and 22 recoveries in the Democratic Republic of the Congo as of 2026-06-10, driven by Bundibugyo strain and among what authorities describe as one of the world's largest outbreaks. Transmission is currently concentrated in Ituri (17 health zones), North Kivu (7 health zones), and a single health zone in South Kivu. The outbreak was officially announced on 15 May, though health officials say silent transmission occurred weeks earlier, hindering response. Healthcare workers face shortages of basic protective equipment; community distrust and resistance have led to attacks on treatment centers and burial teams. article.articleHeadline: Lake Victoria on alert as leaders push for urgent Ebola preparedness measures
article.articleSummary: Ebola risk in Kenya's Lake Victoria basin rises as leaders urge urgent surveillance, screening, and emergency preparedness along cross-border water routes with Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo. As of 2026-06-10, officials warn porous lake borders and high cross-border trade could introduce Ebola into Kenyan counties bordering Lake Victoria, notably along Homa Bay and other lakeside communities. Calls include establishing Ebola screening points at key entry points, quarantine and isolation centres, and robust contact tracing. Legislation cited (Public Health Act Cap 242 and Cap 254) underpins swift ministerial action during outbreaks. Residents demand stronger border controls, better health infrastructure at landing sites, and coordination between border health units and county governments to prevent importation of Ebola.

article.articleSummary: Kenya's Nanyuki witnessed protests against a proposed 50-bed Ebola quarantine facility at Laikipia Air Base, with police shooting dead a protester, Patrick Wahome, and eyewitnesses reporting hooded officers firing live rounds as 19 demonstrators were detained. article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Deadly violence threatens efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak in the DRC, UN says.
article.articleSummary: Violence in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo is hindering Ebola containment, the UN humanitarian office reports as of 2026-06-10. In North Kivu, attacks between May 30 and June 6 in Beni killed at least 40 civilians and obstructed humanitarian access, including the Ebola response. In South Kivu, fighting displaced about 15,000 people to the Miti-Murhesa health zone, where all confirmed Ebola cases in the province are located, heightening concerns about transmission and access to care. The violence is hampering surveillance, contact tracing, and case management, raising the risk of wider spread. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs urged protection of civilians and sustained, unobstructed humanitarian access to support outbreak response.

article.articleSummary: Uganda tightens border surveillance with the Democratic Republic of Congo at Arua’s Vurra border post to curb spread of the Ebola Bundibugyo virus. As of 2026-06-10, Uganda reports 19 confirmed Ebola cases (14 imported, 5 local); 13 admitted, 4 recovered, 2 deaths. Frontline staff, aided by IOM personnel, screen all travellers; only cargo trucks are allowed through after a May directive, reducing cross-border traffic at this busy West Nile point. Screening includes handwashing, temperature checks with infrared thermometers, travel-history interviews, and immediate isolation of suspects, with samples sent to the Uganda Virus Research Institute in Arua and results typically within three hours; three samples tested so far are negative. Response is hampered by shortages of medical supplies (including face masks) and limited infrastructure; border post lacks adequate handwashing facilities and additional screening stations for unofficial routes. To improve compliance, travellers receive screening stickers showing name, date, temperature, and signature.

article.articleSummary: In Karnataka (Bengaluru), HIV-positive cases among men who have sex with men (MSM) rose from 166 in 2023-24 to 412 in 2025-26, per KSAPS data, with 362 in 2024-25. MSM registered under targeted Intervention Programmes (IP) increased from 44,581 (2023-24) to 62,664 (2024-25) and 66,606 (2025-26). The 26-35 age group accounts for the largest share of registrations, followed by 18-25 years. An IP denotes targeted public-health efforts to prevent HIV and other STIs. Padma Basavanthappa, KSAPS Project Director, attributed rising numbers to lack of awareness and misinformation about HIV and sexual health, noting ongoing unsafe-sex practices and gaps in regular HIV testing, partly driven by dating-app use. She called for sustained education and outreach to ensure access to preventive services, reminding that Karnataka records about 12,000–13,000 HIV-positive cases annually across all categories, including MSM, with Bengaluru serving as a major urban center.

article.articleHeadline: Da Dengue a Chikungunya per ogni grado di temperatura in più, sale il rischio infezione
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: From Dengue to Chikungunya, for every degree of temperature increase, infection risk rises.
article.articleSummary: Rising temperatures escalate arbovirus transmission, increasing risks for Dengue, Chikungunya, and West Nile. Each additional 1°C within 23–32°C raises transmissibility by more than 20%. At Verona’s arbovirus congress, Italian and regional experts warn climate anomalies broaden Italy’s exposure to autochthonous foci and urge stronger surveillance, earlier alerts, and public engagement, including personal and household protection in spring and autumn. Studies show: a review of 45 studies in Brazil, Indonesia, and India finds Dengue risk up 16% per 1°C; 1,145 West Nile cases in Italy (2012–2020) link mean air temperature to a 32% per-degree risk increase; a systematic review of 34 experimental studies confirms higher temperatures augment Chikungunya transmission, especially above 28°C. As of 2026-06-10, 133 Dengue cases in Italy, all travel-associated; 13 Chikungunya cases, all imported. The 2024 European Dengue outbreak in Fano reached 223 cases; 2025 Chikungunya totaled 469 cases, 384 autochthonous, and 17 in 2024.

article.articleHeadline: Cảnh báo virus Hanta: Phát hiện chuột trong nhà, người dân cần làm gì?
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Hantavirus Alert: Rats Found in the Home, What Should Residents Do?
article.articleSummary: Hantavirus infection in Vietnam: Rodents, especially rats, are natural hosts; human cases have been sporadic in Vietnam and are not part of a large outbreak. Transmission occurs mainly by inhaling dust or aerosols from rodent urine, droppings, or saliva, or via contact with contaminated surfaces; rodent bites are possible but rare. High-risk settings include dark, damp spaces such as warehouses, barns, granaries, and long-unused areas with rodent activity. Globally, Hantavirus can cause Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome or Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome; Andes virus in South America is the only known human-to-human transmitting strain, with no sustained transmission elsewhere. Early symptoms resemble flu, dengue, or COVID-19—sudden high fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, nausea, and abdominal pain—potentially progressing to respiratory failure or kidney injury. If exposure to rodent waste occurred within 1–4 weeks and symptoms emerge, seek prompt medical evaluation; emphasize rodent control and environmental hygiene to reduce risk.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: A Doctor Says Climate Change Is Driving a Surge in Dengue Fever, Children Are Increasingly Vulnerable
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever surges in Indonesia driven by climate change, with children most vulnerable due to immature immunity. The Aedes aegypti mosquito thrives in warmer temperatures, enabling the disease to spread into highland areas once unaffected. Dr. Riyadi, a pediatric specialist with the Indonesian Pediatric Society (IDAI) and member of its Environmental Health and Climate Change Task Force, warns that rising temperatures expand tropical zones and dengue cases. According to the Ministry of Health’s Directorate General of Disease Prevention and Control, Indonesia reported 131,393 dengue cases and 544 deaths (case fatality rate 0.41%) through October 28, 2025, across 471 regencies/cities in 36 provinces, with fatalities in 196 districts. Long-term solutions emphasize climate mitigation to revert temperatures toward natural baselines, potentially narrowing tropical disease reach. Short-term, IDAI promotes the 3M Plus mosquito-control measures (drain, cover, bury/destroy potential breeding sites) as part of the Pemberantasan Sarang Nyamuk program.

article.articleSummary: Taiwan reports its first domestically confirmed paratyphoid fever case this year: a man in his 50s in Northern Taiwan with no domestic or outbound travel history. He developed fever, headache and body aches in late May, tested positive for Salmonella Paratyphi, was hospitalized, treated with antibiotics, and discharged after eight days. Contacts (1 household member and 7 workplace contacts) yielded negative stool tests; exposure history is under investigation and health authorities are continuing preventive measures and surveillance. Paratyphoid fever is a second-class statutory infectious disease in Taiwan, transmitted mainly via contaminated food or water; incubation 1–10 days; infectious period about 1–2 weeks. This year: 1 local case, 0 imported in 2026; imported cases in 2023–2025 included India (2), Indonesia (1) and Cambodia (1). Globally, ~1.72 million cases in 2023, concentrated in Asia, especially India (≈1.3 million).

article.articleSummary: Indonesia expands the Free Health Check Program (CKG), strengthening tuberculosis (TB) control and upgrading health facilities nationwide. President Prabowo Subianto approved the plan on June 9, 2026, after a fast-track health briefing. The CKG now covers treatment and monitoring for non-communicable diseases—hypertension and diabetes—delivered free via Puskesmas. In 2025, CKG reached over 70 million people; in 2026, more than 42.3 million health checks have been conducted across 38 provinces. TB efforts include expanded case finding, diagnosis, and treatment at primary facilities through an integrated CKG and a one-stop service (OSS) at Puskesmas, enabling same-day screening, diagnosis, and treatment; about 1.08 million TB cases identified this year. Infrastructure upgrades include 66 RSUDs in underserved areas; RSUP Jayapura in Papua completed and ready to inaugurate, serving eastern Indonesia including the Pacific/Oceania. RSUP Riau is ~85% complete (target Dec 2026). 905 essential devices distributed to 258 districts (cath labs, CT, mammography, MRI, Linac).

article.articleSummary: Unsafe food causes 866 million illnesses and 1.52 million deaths worldwide each year, according to WHO and The Lancet Global Health. Children under five bear about 29% of the global burden, with roughly 143,000 deaths in 2021 and nearly triple illness risk versus older individuals due to developing immunity and dehydration from diarrheal disease. Biological hazards drove most illnesses in 2021, but chemical hazards caused nearly 73% of deaths, driven by inorganic arsenic (about 42% of chemical-hazard deaths) and lead (about 31%). article.articleHeadline: West Nile Virus vs Shigella Infection: Key Differences Between The Diseases Raising Concerns In Kerala
article.articleSummary: Kerala faces two infectious threats during the monsoon: West Nile virus (mosquito-borne) and Shigella infection (bacterial). West Nile virus spreads by infected mosquitoes; about 80% of infections are asymptomatic, while ~20% develop West Nile fever with fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pain, rash, fatigue, vomiting or diarrhoea; rare cases in older or immunocompromised individuals progress to encephalitis or meningitis. Shigella spreads through contaminated food or water and direct contact; symptoms include frequent diarrhoea, bloody stools, abdominal cramps, fever, nausea, vomiting, and dehydration, which can be dangerous in young children. Vulnerable groups: West Nile—adults over 60, cancer patients, organ transplant recipients, immunocompromised; Shigella—children under five, elderly, HIV, cancer patients, and those in areas with poor sanitation. Prevention: West Nile—mosquito repellents, protective clothing, eliminating standing water, nets; Shigella—handwashing, safe water, cooking foods, washing produce, sanitation. Early diagnosis and care advised.

The funding, announced June 8, 2026, via Sida, will strengthen national and partner health responses, including deploying 38 experts to Bunia, training more than 150 health workers, with a further 500 already in training, and delivering 17 tonnes of essential humanitarian and medical supplies. This support accompanies Sweden’s rapid-response mechanisms and additional emergency funding of about $100,000 to Trócaire for risk communication in Bunia. The Ebola outbreak, caused by Bundibugyo virus, has been declared a PHEIC on May 17, with no approved vaccine or treatment; rapid measures such as contact tracing and isolation remain crucial.

article.articleSummary: African swine fever (ASF) is spreading in Lao Cai Province, Vietnam, with cases in Gia Hoi, Nghia Tam, Nam Chay, Nam Xe, Duong Quy, Mo Vang, Minh Luong, Khanh Yen, and Van Ban. Local authorities emphasize surveillance, sanitation, prompt reporting, and avoiding the sale of sick pigs to limit spread and safeguard livelihoods and the pig sector.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola in DR Congo; no face shields or boots, health workers without basic facilities.
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease outbreak in DR Congo's eastern provinces of North Kivu and Ituri has reached 550 confirmed cases and 101 deaths, as of early June 2026. Ituri accounts for more than 90% of cases, marking the 17th Ebola infection in the country; the preceding Congolese outbreak occurred in August 2025 with 34 deaths, while 2018–2020 outbreaks caused about 2,300 deaths. The circulating strain is Bundibugyo virus, a rare variant for which no approved vaccine or specific therapy exists. Incubation is typically 2–21 days, with fever, headache, muscle pains, and sore throat, sometimes vomiting and bleeding; severe cases may progress to liver and kidney failure. Transmission occurs via blood and bodily fluids, and via infected animals. Health workers face severe PPE shortages (face shields, boots, gel scarce); PPE stocks are expected within days via IRC. 35 health workers infected, 7 dead.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Pidie Health Office Provides Hantavirus Prevention Education to Inmates at Sigli Women's Prison
article.articleSummary: Pidie Health Office and Sigli Women's Prison (Class IIB) conducted hantavirus prevention education on 10 June 2026 at the prison mosque, engaging staff and inmates. Experts explained hantavirus as a serious disease transmitted through exposure to infected rodent droppings, urine, or saliva, with inhalation of dust from contaminated material as a key route. Early symptoms include sudden high fever, muscle pains, dizziness, and shortness of breath; severe cases may lead to acute respiratory syndrome or kidney failure. Prevention focused on three pillars: maintaining regular environmental sanitation, including corners and storage areas; tightly sealing food and drinks to deter rodents; and proper waste disposal to avoid rodent habitats. The outreach was well-received by prison leadership and aims at early detection and prevention within the facility; the article does not report any cases.

article.articleHeadline: Khỉ Amazon bất ngờ nhiễm căn bệnh tử thần từ con người
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Amazon monkeys suddenly contract a deadly disease from humans.
article.articleSummary: HBV, the human hepatitis B virus, has been detected in New World monkeys in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest for the first time. Researchers from the University of Salford and the Federal University of Amazonas analyzed blood and liver tissue from 88 individuals across 28 primate species in two contrasting zones: deforestation-impacted Rondônia and Mato Grosso, and the largely pristine Upper Japurá River region in Amazonas state. HBV was found in 17 of 49 primates living near human activity, with viral genomes nearly identical to strains circulating in local humans; all 39 monkeys from isolated habitats tested negative. This suggests humans may be the source of cross-species transmission, potentially via pet-keeping of infant monkeys or expanding settlements encroaching on forests. While HBV remains a major human pathogen causing over a million deaths annually, its effects on Amazonian monkeys are unknown. Further controlled studies are needed.

article.articleHeadline: AERIS, Identifikasi Zona Risiko Tinggi Demam Berdarah Karya Mahasiswa ITS - Suara Merdeka Surabaya
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: AERIS, Identification of High-Risk Dengue Fever Zones by ITS Students - Suara Merdeka Surabaya
article.articleSummary: Five Surabaya districts (Tambaksari, Rungkut, Tandes, Sawahan, Semampir) are identified as high-risk zones for dengue fever by ITS's Aedes Aegypti Environmental Risk System (AERIS). The system uses WebGIS and machine learning to predict dengue risk, drawing on 2019-2024 dengue case data from the Surabaya City Health Office, rainfall, topography, population density, standing-water points, and six additional variables. Predictive models include Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, and Negative Binomial Regression; integrating multiple factors enhances risk estimation. Validation on March 2025 data correctly highlighted nine of ten districts with the highest cases; Bubutan was not identified, likely due to a transient local cluster. AERIS also delivers an interactive WebGIS map showing dengue distribution, rainfall, healthcare facilities, and district-level risk, accessible at aeris.geowebgis.id. The team aims to shift from reactive to preventive public health by prioritizing flood control and mosquito breeding-site elimination.

article.articleHeadline: The World Cup could be a petri dish for disease. Wastewater could sound the alarm
article.articleSummary: During the 2026 FIFA World Cup across 16 host cities in three countries in North America, a wastewater surveillance network coordinated by the Health Security Operations Center in Washington, D.C., will monitor community sewage for disease signals to forecast outbreaks. The system targets measles, SARS-CoV-2, influenza, dengue, and Ebola, the latter tied to an ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Wastewater data can reveal community transmission days to weeks before hospital cases rise, allowing earlier vaccination, isolation, and treatment. The public health intelligence hub partners with wastewater sites, biotech firms (notably Verily Health), genomics labs, and local health departments to deliver daily reports and risk notices. Verily’s dashboards track five pathogens: SARS-CoV-2, influenza, measles, RSV, and norovirus, using rapid PCR testing and genome sequencing to refine situational awareness for host cities and cross-country spread.

article.articleHeadline: Shigella Infection: ಏನಿದು ಶಿಗೆಲ್ಲೋಸಿಸ್ ಸೋಂಕು? ಕೇರಳದಲ್ಲಿ ಹೊಸ ವೈರಲ್ ಸೋಂಕಿಗೆ ಜನ ಹೆದರುತ್ತಿರುವುದಕ್ಕೆ ಕಾರಣವೇನು?
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Shigella Infection: What is Shigellosis infection? Why are people in Kerala fearing the new viral infection?
article.articleSummary: Kerala reports 85 lab-confirmed Shigellosis cases and over 70 suspected as of June 7, 2026, with higher transmission in Wayanad, Kozhikode, Alappuzha, and Malappuram districts. Two pediatric deaths have occurred this year, and in Wayanad two children at Mar Baselios School tested positive. Shigella infection spreads rapidly via contaminated food, water, and poor hygiene. It is especially dangerous for children under five, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals; adults typically experience self-limiting illness. Symptoms usually appear 1–2 days after exposure and include fever, diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, blood in stool, stomach pain, and frequent urge to defecate. The Trump administration has proposed a quarantine and treatment facility at a U.S. military base in Kenya for Americans who may have been exposed, drawing criticism and legal pushback. The piece recalls the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak (over 28,000 cases, more than 11,000 deaths; ~39% fatality) and argues that containment at the source is essential. It notes that the United States dismantled much of its public health infrastructure in the past 17 months; USAID is gone, CDC budget constraints, and withdrawal from the WHO. Transmission is mostly non-airborne, requiring contact with bodily fluids, and the disease may take up to 21 days to show symptoms. Airport screening and barrier methods offer limited benefits; risk-based containment mirrors aviation security and is the recommended priority.

article.articleSummary: US Ebola patient treated at Berlin Charité after contracting the Bundibugyo variant in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where he worked as a physician and cared for a patient who died. Transport to Germany occurred about eight days post-exposure; on arrival he showed disorientation and a very high viral load in mucosal and respiratory tissues, with hours before transfer described as life-threatening. His wife and four children, asymptomatic, were quarantined in a separate area of the same unit. The patient received an experimental MBP134 monoclonal antibody cocktail (intravenous, not yet approved; Phase 1) plus Remdesivir, which was also given to his family as Post-Exposure Prophylaxis. After roughly two weeks, he was discharged; treatment costs were in the low seven figures. The case highlights limited MBP134 data, concerns about Bundibugyo infections, and the need for better preparedness and access to experimental therapies and testing.

article.articleHeadline: Fighting pests, infectious disease can mean sterilizing bugs
article.articleSummary: Sterile insect technique (SIT) uses radiated sterile males to suppress pest populations and slows vector-borne disease spread. The article highlights screwworms, which infest livestock and can infect humans; sterilized male screwworm flies released to prevent hatching eggs. Repeated releases in Singapore reduced dengue risk; China, Singapore, Mexico have used sterile mosquitoes. Challenges include high rearing costs, ecological safety concerns, and not being suitable for all species; raising mosquitoes at scale remains difficult.

Ebola is a severe, often deadly disease caused by Ebola viruses. Transmission occurs through contact with blood, bodily fluids, or tissues of an infected person; contact with infected animals (bats and primates); and touching contaminated objects. Symptoms appear 2–21 days after exposure and begin with fever, fatigue, headache, muscle and joint pains, and sore throat, followed by vomiting, diarrhea, rash, abdominal pain, and possible bleeding in severe cases. Most outbreaks are in Africa; isolated imported/exported cases occur mainly among travelers or health workers.

article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo ebolavirus drives an active Ebola outbreak in the DRC with spread to Uganda; no approved vaccine and a case fatality around 50%. About 1,000 suspected cases and over 200 suspected deaths are reported, with additional detections in Uganda and South Sudan and patients under observation in Italy and Brazil. An American who tested positive was evacuated to Germany for treatment, later discharged and recovering. The International Rescue Committee warns response is hampered by delayed detection, low contact tracing (roughly 20% of contacts traced), and diagnostic cartridge shortages causing testing backlogs. Symptoms typically begin 2–21 days after infection: fever, fatigue, muscle pain and headache, followed by vomiting, diarrhea and bleeding in severe cases. Transmission requires direct contact with infected fluids; it is not airborne. With the DRC team based in Houston, CDC and FIFA coordinate screening and containment; a breakdown could disrupt the World Cup.

article.articleHeadline: Czechy: Amerykański lekarz, który miał kontakt z ebolą, wypisany ze szpitala w Pradze
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Czech Republic: American doctor who had contact with Ebola discharged from hospital in Prague.
article.articleSummary: American doctor Patrick LaRochelle, who had potential Ebola exposure, was discharged from Prague’s infectious-diseases clinic as of 2026-06-10. He arrived May 21 from Africa by medical flight, then by ambulance to the Prague clinic, spending two weeks in a sealed biobox with staff in full protective gear. In interviews, LaRochelle said isolation created distance from his family, though he spoke daily by phone and advised colleagues at the German Red Cross (DRK) from abroad. He expressed willingness to return for medical missions and praised Czech care. Czechia had several patients under suspicion of Ebola or other haemorrhagic fevers, but none were confirmed; in May a Czech soldier on a UN mission in the DRC was quarantined. Ebola spreads by contact; symptoms include fever, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle pains, and bleeding. Vaccines exist for some strains, but not for the strain in the DRC and Uganda.

article.articleHeadline: Εφιάλτης δίχως τέλος στο Κονγκό: Εκτός ελέγχου ο Έμπολα με εκατοντάδες κρούσματα εν μέσω ένοπλων συγκρούσεων
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: An endless nightmare in Congo: Ebola out of control with hundreds of cases amid armed clashes.
article.articleSummary: In the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ebola cases attributed to the Bundibugyo strain have reached 598 confirmed, with 115 deaths and 22 recoveries, as of 2026-06-10. The outbreak spans Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu provinces amid ongoing armed clashes, making it one of the world’s largest Ebola events. Officials say the virus was confirmed in mid-May but circulated undetected for weeks, delaying response. It has affected 17 health zones in Ituri, 7 in North Kivu, and 1 in South Kivu. Social distrust and violence against medical centers and burial teams hinder containment. Authorities urge the public to seek prompt medical care for fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or severe fatigue, and to stop attacks on health workers. Healthcare staff report severe PPE shortages, risking safety and potentially fueling transmission.

article.articleHeadline: الصحة العالمية: توقف اختبارات الإيبولا في 3 مختبرات بالكونغو بسبب نقص الإمدادات
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: World Health Organization: Ebola testing halted in 3 laboratories in the Democratic Republic of the Congo due to supply shortages.
article.articleSummary: Ebola testing has halted in three laboratories in the Democratic Republic of the Congo due to supply shortages, delaying analyses in Bukavu and Luero (South Kivu) and Goma (North Kivu) while awaiting necessary reagents to resume testing of accumulated samples. Congo reports about 600 confirmed Ebola cases and 115 deaths; in neighboring Uganda, 19 cases and 2 deaths have been recorded. Security challenges and armed conflict in the most affected areas are slowing surveillance and laboratory work. Professor Jean-Jacques Muyimbi expressed cautious optimism that testing capacity will improve but criticized aspects of the response and urged engagement with affected communities to build trust and protect residents. All three labs remain reliant on reagent deliveries to restart Ebola virus testing.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola toll in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
article.articleSummary: 635 laboratory-confirmed Ebola cases and 127 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo as of 2026-06-10, with 8 new recoveries—7 in Nyankondi and 1 in Mongbawulo—bringing total recoveries to 30. A further 406 contacts completed the 21-day follow-up period. The Ebola outbreak in the DRC and Uganda remains active, and on May 17 the World Health Organization declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, with regional spread risk deemed high. The report underscores ongoing surveillance and follow-up among contacts as authorities monitor the outbreak across the DRC and neighboring Uganda.

article.articleHeadline: T&T intensifies border screening for Ebola
article.articleSummary: On 10 June 2026, Trinidad and Tobago announced intensified border controls in response to the Ebola outbreak in parts of Central Africa. All travelers arriving from Ebola-affected countries—Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan—will undergo health screening and may face quarantine. The Health Ministry disclosed the measures, and the health minister urged citizens to reconsider travel to high-risk countries. A mandatory 21-day active monitoring protocol applies to individuals arriving after visiting or transiting through the affected nations, reinforcing surveillance and early detection to prevent importation of Ebola. These measures are described as strict border management measures. The measures accompany ongoing border management amid the Central Africa Ebola outbreak.

article.articleHeadline: Unstoppable Virus Poses Major Threat to Upcoming World Cup Without Vaccine Solution - Internewscast Journal
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) threatens the upcoming World Cup, with nearly 1,000 potential cases and over 200 probable fatalities. Cases are rising in Uganda and South Sudan, while Italy and Brazil monitor; an American patient tested positive and was transported to Germany for treatment, later discharged and recovering. The International Rescue Committee warns detection is slow and contact tracing insufficient, with only about 20 percent of contacts traced and shortages of diagnostic cartridges causing testing backlogs. Ebola symptoms begin 2–21 days after infection—fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, then vomiting, diarrhea and bleeding—and spread through direct contact with infected bodily fluids. DRC's World Cup team will be based in Houston and self-isolate; containment failures could disrupt group play. A Level 3 U.S. travel warning remains for the DRC, with Americans arriving from DRC/Uganda/South Sudan rerouted to four airports for enhanced screening. The CDC is coordinating with FIFA.

article.articleHeadline: WHO kêu gọi phối hợp khống chế dịch Ebola
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: WHO calls for coordinated efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak continues in the border region between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Uganda, with 598 laboratory-confirmed cases and 115 deaths reported by June 9, 2026. WHO assesses the cross-border spread as a 'very high' risk. WHO Director-General Tedros praised Uganda’s rapid response, including border screening, surveillance, testing, case management, and cross-border coordination. Uganda plans to deploy more health workers, establish a 50-bed treatment facility, and strengthen cross-border surveillance to curb transmission. In Nigeria, President Bola Tinubu establishes a dedicated rapid-response force to assess preparedness and develop strategies for Ebola and other health threats. The situation is worsened by ongoing insecurity in eastern DRC, hindering responder access. WHO coordinates with partners and plans to mobilize $518 million to boost preparedness, detection, and response. EU official Hadja Lahbib calls for a ceasefire to improve aid access.

article.articleHeadline: Secretaria de Saúde de São Paulo investiga segundo caso suspeito de ebola - Ser Saúde
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: São Paulo Health Department investigates second suspected Ebola case - Ser Saúde.
article.articleSummary: Two Ebola-related investigations in São Paulo, Brazil, as of 2026-06-10. A 31-year-old Brazilian woman who worked in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo arrived in Brazil on June 6 and developed fever and diarrhea by June 9. She is hospitalized at Instituto de Infectologia Emílio Ribas in a single isolation bed with biosafety protocols in place; Ebola status not confirmed yet, and a formal case investigation is ongoing per state health department criteria. A prior June 1 case, a 37-year-old male immigrant from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, tested negative for Ebola; he had fever and was isolated at Emílio Ribas. Earlier testing confirmed meningococcal meningitis. Ebola is rare per WHO but severe; Brazil/South America risk is considered very low by experts.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: Authorities urged to protect children amid Ebola outbreak - ACP
article.articleSummary: Kinshasa, June 10, 2026: An appeal to authorities, scientists and the community to protect children from Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) as the outbreak continues in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Solange Ghonda, Special Ambassador for Children, urged intensified research and mobilization to save lives and protect vulnerable children, describing Ebola as a disease occurring exclusively on the African continent. She called for mobilizing the international community and leveraging women as the primary communication relay for preventive measures, especially in remote villages, to encourage rapid adoption of life-saving practices. Better information, she said, enables the population to act to prevent new cases from becoming outbreaks. Combating Ebola requires solidarity, innovation and partnerships among academic institutions, governments and international organizations, with WHO declaring the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern.

article.articleHeadline: गाजियाबाद में पोलियो वायरस का अलर्ट, डूंडाहेड़ा STP से जुड़ी कॉलोनियों पर नजर; विदेशियों का तैयार होगा ब्यौरा - ghaziabad vdpv poliovirus found in sewage survey underway
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Polio virus alert in Ghaziabad, monitoring colonies linked to Dundahera STP; a report on foreigners will be prepared — Ghaziabad VDPV poliovirus found in sewage; survey underway.
article.articleSummary: As of 10 June 2026, Ghaziabad detects vaccine-derived poliovirus Type 1 (VDPV-1) in sewage from the Dundahera sewage treatment plant (STP), prompting a polio alert. Health authorities are mapping Dundahera-linked colonies and conducting door-to-door surveys in 12 areas, targeting over 150,000 children under five. Sewage from Crossing Republic, Dundahera, Siddharth Vihar, Pratap Vihar, Raj Nagar, KavNagar, Shastri Nagar, Bajaria, Bulandshahr Road industrial area, Vijaynagar, and parts of Trans Hindon is treated at the STP (70 MLD capacity). Investigations seek the virus source, including whether a foreign traveler or child’s stool contributed; data on hotels and international stays over the past year are being compiled. A 107-team collaboration of state and local officials, with WHO surveillance, is underway. Aimed at 100% vaccination coverage, a polio campaign starts 28 June. Report by Dr. Sachin Chandra Vaishy, CMO.
